tools.description: List the contents of a directory. Result will have the name of the child. If the name ends in /, it's a folder, otherwise a file

path.description: The absolute path to the directory to list.

tools.name: memory
tools.description: Store a fact about the codebase in memory, so that it can be used in future code generation or review tasks. The fact should be a clear and concise statement about the codebase conventions, structure, logic, or usage. It may be based on the code itself, or on information provided by the user.

subject.description: The topic to which this memory relates. 1-2 words. Examples: naming conventions, testing practices, documentation, logging, authentication, sanitization, error handling.

fact.description: A clear and short description of a fact about the codebase or a convention used in the codebase. Must be less than 200 characters. Examples: Use JWT for authentication. Follow PEP 257 docstring conventions. Use single quotes for strings in Python. Use Winston for logging.

citations.description: The source of this fact, such as a file and line number in the codebase (e.g., path/file.go:123). If the convention is not explicitly stated in the codebase, you can point at several examples that illustrate it, selecting the most diverse set of examples you can find (e.g. from multiple files or contexts). If the fact is based on user input, the citations should be User input: followed by the contents of the input.

reason.description: A clear and detailed explanation of the reason behind storing this fact. Must be at least 2-3 sentences long, and include which future tasks this fact will be useful for and why it is important to remember this fact.

category.description: The type of memory being stored. This can be bootstrap_and_build (info about how to bootstrap and build the project), user_preferences (preferences of the user, such as coding style, tabs vs. spaces, favorite libraries, etc.), general (file independent facts), or file_specific (information about a specific file in the codebase).

tools.name: multi_replace_string_in_file
tools.description: This tool allows you to apply multiple replace_string_in_file operations in a single call, which is more efficient than calling replace_string_in_file multiple times. It takes an array of replacement operations and applies them sequentially. Each replacement operation has the same parameters as replace_string_in_file: filePath, oldString, newString, and explanation. This tool is ideal when you need to make multiple edits across different files or multiple edits in the same file. The tool will provide a summary of successful and failed operations.

explanation.description: A brief explanation of what the multi-replace operation will accomplish.

replacements.description: An array of replacement operations to apply sequentially.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the file to edit.

oldString.description: The exact literal text to replace, preferably unescaped. Include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. If this string is not the exact literal text or does not match exactly, this replacement will fail.

newString.description: The exact literal text to replace `oldString` with, preferably unescaped. Provide the EXACT text. Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.

tools.name: open_simple_browser
tools.description: Preview a website or open a URL in the editor's Simple Browser. Useful for quickly viewing locally hosted websites, demos, or resources without leaving the coding environment.

url.description: The website URL to preview or open in the Simple Browser inside the editor. Must be either an http or https URL

tools.name: read_file
tools.description:
Read the contents of a file.

You must specify the line range you're interested in. Line numbers are 1-indexed. If the file contents returned are insufficient for your task, you may call this tool again to retrieve more content. Prefer reading larger ranges over doing many small reads.

filePath.description: The absolute path of the file to read.

startLine.description: The line number to start reading from, 1-based.

endLine.description: The inclusive line number to end reading at, 1-based.

tools.name: read_notebook_cell_output
tools.description: This tool will retrieve the output for a notebook cell from its most recent execution or restored from disk. The cell may have output even when it has not been run in the current kernel session. This tool has a higher token limit for output length than the runNotebookCell tool.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the notebook file with the cell to run, or the URI of a untitled, not yet named, file, such as `untitled:Untitled-1.ipynb

cellId.description: The ID of the cell for which output should be retrieved.

tools.name: replace_string_in_file
tools.description:
This is a tool for making edits in an existing file in the workspace. For moving or renaming files, use run in terminal tool with the 'mv' command instead. For larger edits, split them into smaller edits and call the edit tool multiple times to ensure accuracy. Before editing, always ensure you have the context to understand the file's contents and context. To edit a file, provide: 1) filePath (absolute path), 2) oldString (MUST be the exact literal text to replace including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc), and 3) newString (MUST be the exact literal text to replace \`oldString\` with (also including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc.). Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.). Each use of this tool replaces exactly ONE occurrence of oldString.

CRITICAL for \`oldString\`: Must uniquely identify the single instance to change. Include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. If this string matches multiple locations, or does not match exactly, the tool will fail. Never use 'Lines 123-456 omitted' from summarized documents or ...existing code... comments in the oldString or newString.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the file to edit.

oldString.description: The exact literal text to replace, preferably unescaped. For single replacements (default), include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. For multiple replacements, specify expected_replacements parameter. If this string is not the exact literal text (i.e. you escaped it) or does not match exactly, the tool will fail.

newString.description: The exact literal text to replace `old_string` with, preferably unescaped. Provide the EXACT text. Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.

tools.name: run_notebook_cell
tools.description: This is a tool for running a code cell in a notebook file directly in the notebook editor. The output from the execution will be returned. Code cells should be run as they are added or edited when working through a problem to bring the kernel state up to date and ensure the code executes successfully. Code cells are ready to run and don't require any pre-processing. If asked to run the first cell in a notebook, you should run the first code cell since markdown cells cannot be executed. NOTE: Avoid executing Markdown cells or providing Markdown cell IDs, as Markdown cells cannot be  executed.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the notebook file with the cell to run, or the URI of a untitled, not yet named, file, such as `untitled:Untitled-1.ipynb

reason.description: An optional explanation of why the cell is being run. This will be shown to the user before the tool is run and is not necessary if it's self-explanatory.

cellId.description: The ID for the code cell to execute. Avoid providing markdown cell IDs as nothing will be executed.

continueOnError.description: Whether or not execution should continue for remaining cells if an error is encountered. Default to false unless instructed otherwise.

tools.name: run_vscode_command
tools.description: Run a command in VS Code. Use this tool to run a command in Visual Studio Code as part of a new workspace creation process only.

commandId.description: The ID of the command to execute. This should be in the format <command>.

name.description: The name of the command to execute. This should be a clear and concise description of the command.

args.description: The arguments to pass to the command. This should be an array of strings.

tools.name: semantic_search
tools.description: Run a natural language search for relevant code or documentation comments from the user's current workspace. Returns relevant code snippets from the user's current workspace if it is large, or the full contents of the workspace if it is small.

query.description: The query to search the codebase for. Should contain all relevant context. Should ideally be text that might appear in the codebase, such as function names, variable names, or comments.

tools.name: switch_agent
tools.description:
Switch to the Plan agent before exploring the codebase and refining implementation of a feature. The Plan agent provides specialized tools to explore the codebase, understand system architecture, and iterate with the user through clarifying questions and context gathering.

PLAN AGENT BEHAVIOR:
The Plan agent is a specialized assistant designed for research, exploration, and planning. It:
- Has access to powerful codebase exploration tools (search, read files, list directories, find symbols)
- Can ask clarifying questions to understand requirements better
- Proposes implementation approaches and validates them with the user
- Gathers comprehensive context before suggesting changes
- Handles complex, multi-file refactoring and architectural decisions
- Summarizes findings and creates detailed plans for implementation

EXAMPLES OF WHEN TO SWITCH TO PLAN:
- "I want to refactor the data flow in this component" → Plan can explore the component dependencies
- "How should I integrate this new feature?" → Plan can investigate the architecture and propose approaches
- "Find all usages of this pattern and suggest a better way" → Plan can search comprehensively and report findings
- "I need to migrate from X to Y" → Plan can understand current structure and propose migration strategy

USE THIS TOOL IMMEDIATELY AND PROACTIVELY BEFORE ANY OTHER TOOL CALLS OR CODE EXPLORATION WHEN:
- The user's request is ambiguous, underspecified, or could be interpreted multiple ways
- You need to explore the codebase, gather context, or understand the architecture - CODE EXPLORATION IS THE PLAN AGENT'S PRIMARY RESPONSIBILITY
- The task involves multiple files, complex refactoring, or architectural decisions
- You want to propose an approach and validate it with the user before implementing
- The user explicitly asks for a plan or wants to discuss the approach first
- You're uncertain whether you have sufficient context to confidently implement the complete change

CRITICAL: If you are about to call any code exploration tools (readFile, findTextInFiles, searchCodebase, listDirectory, etc.), STOP immediately and switch to the Plan agent first. Code exploration, context gathering, and architectural understanding belong to the Plan agent, not the inline editor.

You should ONLY skip using this tool when:
- The task is completely straightforward with explicit, detailed implementation instructions
- You already have complete and specific context about exactly what needs to change and where
- The user has explicitly instructed you to skip planning and just make the change

agentName.description: The name of the agent to switch to. Currently only 'Plan' is supported.

tools.name: test_failure
tools.description: Includes test failure information in the prompt.

tools.name: vscode_searchExtensions_internal
tools.description: This is a tool for browsing Visual Studio Code Extensions Marketplace. It allows the model to search for extensions and retrieve detailed information about them. The model should use this tool whenever it needs to discover extensions or resolve information about known ones. To use the tool, the model has to provide the category of the extensions, relevant search keywords, or known extension IDs. Note that search results may include false positives, so reviewing and filtering is recommended.

category.description: The category of extensions to search for

ids.description: The ids of the extensions to search for

tools.name: await_terminal
tools.description: Wait for a background terminal command to complete. Returns the output, exit code, or timeout status.

id.description: The ID of the terminal to await (returned by run_in_terminal when isBackground=true).

timeout.description: Timeout in milliseconds. If the command does not complete within this time, returns the output collected so far with a timeout indicator. Use 0 for no timeout.

tools.name: create_and_run_task
tools.description: Creates and runs a build, run, or custom task for the workspace by generating or adding to a tasks.json file based on the project structure (such as package.json or README.md). If the user asks to build, run, launch and they have no tasks.json file, use this tool. If they ask to create or add a task, use this tool.

workspaceFolder.description: The absolute path of the workspace folder where the tasks.json file will be created.

task.description: The task to add to the new tasks.json file.

type.description: The type of the task. The only supported value is 'shell'.

command.description: The shell command to run for the task. Use this to specify commands for building or running the application.

args.description: The arguments to pass to the command.

isBackground.description: Whether the task runs in the background without blocking the UI or other tasks. Set to true for long-running processes like watch tasks or servers that should continue executing without requiring user attention. When false, the task will block the terminal until completion.

problemMatcher.description: The problem matcher to use to parse task output for errors and warnings. Can be a predefined matcher like '$tsc' (TypeScript), '$eslint - stylish', '$gcc', etc., or a custom pattern defined in tasks.json. This helps VS Code display errors in the Problems panel and enables quick navigation to error locations.

group.description: The group to which the task belongs.

tools.name: get_terminal_output
tools.description: Get the output of a terminal command previously started with run_in_terminal

id.description: The ID of the terminal to check.

tools.name: kill_terminal
tools.description: Kill a terminal by its ID. Use this to clean up terminals that are no longer needed (e.g., after stopping a server or when a long-running task completes). The terminal ID is returned by run_in_terminal when isBackground=true.

id.description: The ID of the background terminal to kill (returned by run_in_terminal when isBackground=true).

tools.name: manage_todo_list
tools.description:
Manage a structured todo list to track progress and plan tasks throughout your coding session. Use this tool VERY frequently to ensure task visibility and proper planning.

When to use this tool:
- Complex multi-step work requiring planning and tracking
- When user provides multiple tasks or requests (numbered/comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions that require multiple steps
- BEFORE starting work on any todo (mark as in-progress)
- IMMEDIATELY after completing each todo (mark completed individually)
- When breaking down larger tasks into smaller actionable steps
- To give users visibility into your progress and planning

When NOT to use:
- Single, trivial tasks that can be completed in one step
- Purely conversational/informational requests
- When just reading files or performing simple searches

CRITICAL workflow:
1. Plan tasks by writing todo list with specific, actionable items
2. Mark ONE todo as in-progress before starting work
3. Complete the work for that specific todo
4. Mark that todo as completed IMMEDIATELY
5. Move to next todo and repeat

Todo states:
- not-started: Todo not yet begun
- in-progress: Currently working (limit ONE at a time)
- completed: Finished successfully

IMPORTANT: Mark todos completed as soon as they are done. Do not batch completions.

todoList.description: Complete array of all todo items. Must include ALL items - both existing and new.

id.description: Unique identifier for the todo. Use sequential numbers starting from 1.

title.description: Concise action-oriented todo label (3-7 words). Displayed in UI.

status.description: not-started: Not begun | in-progress: Currently working (max 1) | completed: Fully finished with no blockers

tools.name: run_in_terminal
tools.description:
This tool allows you to execute PowerShell commands in a persistent terminal session, preserving environment variables, working directory, and other context across multiple commands.

Command Execution:
- Prefer ; when chaining commands on one line
- Prefer pipelines | for object-based data flow
- Never create a sub-shell (eg. powershell -c "command") unless explicitly asked

Directory Management:
- Prefer relative paths when navigating directories, only use absolute when the path is far away or the current cwd is not expected
- Remember when isBackground=false is specified, that the shell and cwd are reused until it is moved to the background
- Use $PWD or Get-Location for current directory
- Use Push-Location/Pop-Location for directory stack

Program Execution:
- Supports .NET, Python, Node.js, and other executables
- Install modules via Install-Module, Install-Package
- Use Get-Command to verify cmdlet/function availability

Background Processes:
- For long-running tasks (e.g., servers), set isBackground=true
- Returns a terminal ID for checking status and runtime later
- Use Start-Job for background PowerShell jobs

Output Management:
- Output is automatically truncated if longer than 60KB to prevent context overflow
- Use Select-Object, Where-Object, Format-Table to filter output
- Use -First/-Last parameters to limit results
- For pager commands, add | Out-String or | Format-List

Best Practices:
- Use proper cmdlet names instead of aliases in scripts
- Quote paths with spaces: "C:\Path With Spaces"
- Prefer PowerShell cmdlets over external commands when available
- Prefer idiomatic PowerShell like Get-ChildItem instead of dir or ls for file listings
- Use Test-Path to check file/directory existence
- Be specific with Select-Object properties to avoid excessive output
- Avoid printing credentials unless absolutely required

command.description: The command to run in the terminal.

explanation.description: A one-sentence description of what the command does. This will be shown to the user before the command is run.

goal.description: A short description of the goal or purpose of the command (e.g., "Install dependencies", "Start development server").

isBackground.description:
Whether the command starts a background process.

- If true, a new shell will be spawned where the cwd is the workspace directory and will run asynchronously in the background and you will not see the output.

- If false, a single shell is shared between all non-background terminals where the cwd starts at the workspace directory and is remembered until that terminal is moved to the background, the tool call will block on the command finishing and only then you will get the output.

Examples of background processes: building in watch mode, starting a server. You can check the output of a background process later on by using get_terminal_output.

timeout.description: An optional timeout in milliseconds. When provided, the tool will stop tracking the command after this duration and return the output collected so far. Be conservative with the timeout duration, give enough time that the command would complete on a low-end machine. Use 0 for no timeout. If it's not clear how long the command will take then use 0 to avoid prematurely terminating it, never guess too low.

tools.name: runSubagent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks autonomously. This tool is good at researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries, use this agent to perform the search for you.

- Agents do not run async or in the background, you will wait for the agent's result.
- When the agent is done, it will return a single message back to you. The result returned by the agent is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Each agent invocation is stateless. You will not be able to send additional messages to the agent, nor will the agent be able to communicate with you outside of its final report. Therefore, your prompt should contain a highly detailed task description for the agent to perform autonomously and you should specify exactly what information the agent should return back to you in its final and only message to you.
- The agent's outputs should generally be trusted
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since it is not aware of the user's intent
- If the user asks for a certain agent, you MUST provide that EXACT agent name (case-sensitive) to invoke that specific agent.

prompt.description: A detailed description of the task for the agent to perform

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

agentName.description: Optional name of a specific agent to invoke. If not provided, uses the current agent.

tools.name: terminal_last_command
tools.description: Get the last command run in the active terminal.

tools.name: terminal_selection
tools.description: Get the current selection in the active terminal.

tools.name: activate_data_analysis_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is designed to facilitate efficient data analysis workflows. The primary focus is on ensuring that users follow best practices when analyzing data files, starting with the 'data_analysis_best_practice' tool. This tool provides a foundational understanding of the analysis workflow, which is crucial before utilizing any other tools in this group. The 'check_panel_open' tool allows users to verify if a 'Data Viewer' panel is currently active, providing essential information about the data source and its status. 

Once the panel status is confirmed, users can leverage the 'get_table_schema' tool to retrieve the structure of the data, including metadata such as row and column counts, names, and inferred data types. This is particularly useful for understanding the dataset before performing any operations. The 'read_rows' tool enables users to extract specific rows from the data, either from the open panel or directly from a file, with options for filtering columns, making it easy to focus on relevant information. 

For users looking to save their analysis results, the 'export_panel_data' tool allows for exporting the current data state to a designated folder in the workspace, ensuring that data can be preserved for future reference or further analysis. This tool also respects the original file format, maintaining consistency in data handling. 

Together, these tools create a cohesive suite for data analysis, guiding users through the necessary steps to ensure thorough and accurate data examination, while also providing mechanisms for data management and export.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: activate_ai_agent_evaluation_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is focused on the evaluation and development of AI agents and applications. It provides a structured approach to converting declarative agent specifications into executable code, ensuring that best practices are followed during the coding process. The 'convert_declarative_agent_to_code' tool is essential for developers looking to translate their specifications into runnable code, offering guidance and code samples in Python or .NET. 

The 'evaluation_planner' tool serves as a critical starting point for any evaluation process, guiding users through a multi-turn conversation to clarify essential details such as evaluation metrics, test datasets, and runtime requirements. This ensures that all necessary information is gathered before proceeding with evaluation code generation. 

Once the planning phase is complete, users can utilize the 'get_evaluation_code_gen_best_practices' tool to access best practices specifically tailored for generating evaluation code, ensuring that the evaluation process is both effective and efficient. Additionally, the 'get_agent_model_code_sample' tool provides valuable code snippets for AI agent and model development, facilitating quicker implementation and reducing the likelihood of errors. 

Lastly, the 'get_tracing_code_gen_best_practices' tool offers guidance on best practices for tracing operations within AI applications, which is crucial for debugging and performance monitoring. Collectively, these tools empower developers to create, evaluate, and refine AI agents with a focus on best practices and structured methodologies.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: ai-mlstudio-get_trend_data
tools.description: Gets the evaluation trend data from the currently focused Evaluation Trend Analysis view (either standalone panel or embedded trend in Data Viewer). Returns: dataPoints (array of files with fileName, filePath, and metrics - metric values are AVERAGED across selected rows), selectedMetrics (list of metrics being compared), jsonArrayProperty (for JSON files, indicates which array property the data comes from), selectedRows (1-based row indices used for averaging, undefined means all rows), totalRows (total row count). Use this tool when the user asks to analyze or discuss evaluation trends. The tool automatically detects which trend view is currently active/focused.

tools.name: activate_migration_assessment_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is designed to facilitate the assessment and reporting of migration readiness and outcomes. The 'migration_assessmentReport' tool provides a detailed webview interface that displays the results of a migration assessment, including identified issues, recommendations for improvement, and an analysis of readiness for Azure migration. This tool is essential for users to understand the implications of their migration efforts and to plan accordingly based on the assessment results.

The 'migration_assessmentReportsList' tool complements the first by allowing users to access a list of all assessment reports generated. This is particularly useful for tracking multiple assessments over time, enabling users to compare results and monitor progress in addressing identified issues.

Lastly, the 'uploadAssessSummaryReport' tool serves as a means to upload the summary report of the assessment to a GitHub issue. This integration allows for seamless collaboration and documentation of the migration process, ensuring that all stakeholders have access to the assessment findings and can contribute to discussions or resolutions.

Together, these tools create a comprehensive workflow for managing migration assessments, from initial evaluation to reporting and collaboration. Users can efficiently assess their migration readiness, document findings, and engage with their teams to address any challenges identified during the assessment process.

Overall, this group of tools is invaluable for organizations looking to migrate to Azure, providing them with the necessary insights and documentation to make informed decisions and streamline their migration efforts.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.description: This tool retrieves extension configuration settings from VS Code. Use this tool when you need to check configuration values for the GitHub Copilot app modernization extension.

tools.name: activate_notebook_kernel_configuration_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is designed to facilitate the configuration and management of notebook environments by allowing users to select and start different types of kernels. The 'configure_python_notebook' tool specifically enables users to select a Python kernel, which is essential for running Python code within a notebook interface. This is particularly useful for data science, machine learning, and general programming tasks where Python is the primary language of choice. On the other hand, the 'configure_non_python_notebook' tool allows users to select and start a kernel for notebooks that may support other programming languages, thus providing flexibility for users who work with multiple languages or frameworks. 

Together, these tools empower users to tailor their notebook environments to their specific needs, whether they are working on Python-based projects or exploring other programming languages. By enabling the selection of different kernels, users can seamlessly switch between languages and leverage the unique features and libraries available in each. This capability is crucial for collaborative projects where team members may have different language preferences or requirements. 

In summary, these notebook kernel configuration tools enhance the usability and versatility of notebook environments, making them suitable for a wide range of programming tasks and educational purposes. Users can easily manage their coding environments, ensuring that they have the right tools at their disposal for any given project.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: activate_notebook_package_management
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is specifically designed for managing Python packages within Jupyter notebooks. The 'notebook_install_packages' tool allows users to install a specified list of packages directly into the notebook's kernel, ensuring that the necessary libraries are available for executing Python code cells. This is particularly useful for data analysis, machine learning, and scientific computing tasks where specific libraries are required. Users should invoke the 'configure_notebooks' tool prior to using 'notebook_install_packages' to ensure the notebook environment is properly set up.

The 'notebook_list_packages' tool complements the installation functionality by providing a way to list all currently installed packages in the selected kernel. This is essential for users to verify that the required packages are indeed installed and to check for any version discrepancies that may affect code execution.

Together, these tools facilitate a seamless workflow for Python developers and data scientists working within Jupyter notebooks. By allowing easy installation and verification of packages, they help maintain an organized and efficient coding environment.

Users can leverage these tools to quickly adapt their notebook environments to different projects by installing only the necessary packages, thus avoiding clutter and potential conflicts with other libraries. This targeted approach enhances productivity and reduces setup time for new projects.

In summary, the 'notebook_package_management' group provides essential functionalities for package installation and management within Jupyter notebooks, making it an invaluable resource for anyone working in Python-based data science or development environments.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: activate_python_environment_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is designed to facilitate the management and retrieval of details related to Python environments. The tools included are essential for developers working with Python, particularly in environments that utilize virtual environments such as conda or venv. The first tool, 'get_python_environment_details', allows users to obtain comprehensive information about the Python environment associated with a specific file or workspace. This includes the type of environment, the version of Python in use, and a list of all installed packages along with their respective versions. This information is crucial for ensuring compatibility and for troubleshooting issues related to package dependencies.

The second tool, 'get_python_executable_details', complements the first by providing detailed information on how to construct the command needed to execute Python scripts in the terminal. It generates the fully qualified path to the Python executable and outlines the necessary arguments for running Python commands. This is particularly useful for users who need to execute Python scripts in a specific environment without manually searching for the executable path.

Together, these tools streamline the process of managing Python environments, making it easier for developers to switch between different setups and ensure that they are using the correct versions of Python and its packages. By calling 'configure_python_environment' before using either tool, users can ensure that they are working within the intended environment, which enhances the reliability of the information retrieved.

These tools are particularly beneficial in collaborative projects where multiple developers may be using different environments. By providing a clear overview of the environment details, they help maintain consistency across development setups. Additionally, they can assist in onboarding new team members by providing them with the necessary environment configurations and executable paths.

Overall, the 'python_environment_tools' group is an essential resource for Python developers, enabling them to efficiently manage their development environments and execute scripts with confidence.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: configure_python_environment
tools.description: This tool configures a Python environment in the given workspace. ALWAYS Use this tool to set up the user's chosen environment and ALWAYS call this tool before using any other Python related tools or running any Python command in the terminal.

resourcePath.description: The path to the Python file or workspace for which a Python Environment needs to be configured.

tools.name: container-tools_get-config
tools.description: Gets the configuration the user has set for the container and container orchestrator (compose) CLIs, including the correct base commands to use and any environment variables that will be set. This tool **MUST** be called before generating or running any container or container orchestrator CLI commands, to ensure the correct base command is used.

tools.name: activate_github_pull_request_management
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is designed to facilitate the management and retrieval of information related to GitHub pull requests (PRs). The tools included allow users to access detailed information about both active and open pull requests, providing insights into their status, changes made, and associated comments. The 'github-pull-request_activePullRequest' tool specifically focuses on the currently checked-out pull request, offering comprehensive details such as the PR title, description, list of changed files, review comments, and CI results. tools.name: mcp_copilot_upgra_upgrade_authenticate_nuget_feed
tools.description:
Call upgrade_authenticate_nuget_feed to resolve NuGet package authentication failures when restore or build operations fail with access errors.

**When to use this tool:**
- Build or restore operations fail with authentication errors for private NuGet feeds
- Error messages contain NU1301 (unable to load service index for source)
- HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) or 403 (Forbidden) errors when accessing NuGet feeds
- Errors mention "Unable to find package" from Azure DevOps feeds (pkgs.dev.azure.com)
- Package restore fails with "Unable to load the service index" from authenticated feeds

**How this tool works (requires human-in-the-loop):**
1. Invokes the Azure Artifacts credential provider in interactive mode
2. The credential provider outputs authentication instructions (typically a device code and URL)
3. User must manually open the provided URL in a browser and complete authentication
4. After user completes authentication, call this tool again to verify credentials are cached
5. Once credentials are verified, retry the failed operation

**Important:** This tool does NOT automatically open a browser. It provides instructions that the user must follow manually. After the user authenticates, you must call this tool again to verify the credentials are properly cached before retrying the build.

Extract the failing feed URL from error messages to use as the feedUrl parameter.

# Copilot instructions for Tensor-Engine

## Quick orientation ✅

- Languages: **Rust** core (crate: `tensor_engine`) + **Python** bindings (PyO3/maturin). See `Cargo.toml`, `src/`, and `src/lib.rs`.
- High-level architecture: core tensor/autograd in `src/tensor.rs`, ops in `src/ops.rs`, NN layers in `src/nn/*.rs`, IO & loaders in `src/io/*` (SafeTensors and PyTorch loaders), Python surface in `src/lib.rs`.
- Primary patterns to follow: `Module` and `Operation` traits, and PyO3 style wrappers (`PyTensor` in `src/lib.rs`).

## Immediate developer workflows (commands you’ll use) 🔧

- Run unit tests (Rust):
  - cargo test --verbose --workspace
  - For feature matrix: cargo test --verbose --workspace --features "<feature>"
- Build & iterate Python bindings locally (recommended):
  - pip install maturin
  - maturin develop --release --bindings pyo3
  - Build wheel: maturin build --release
- CI-specific notes (see `.github/workflows/ci.yml`):
  - OpenBLAS support via feature `openblas` (Windows CI sets OPENBLAS_DIR)
  - `with_tch` feature needs a compatible libtorch / VC toolchain on Windows
- Docs: build with MkDocs (`scripts/build_docs.ps1` or `./scripts/build_docs.sh`) and preview with `mkdocs serve`.

## Project-specific conventions & rules (must follow) ⚠️

- impl Module must provide `fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut dyn Any`.
  - Verification: `python scripts/verify_as_any_mut.py` (also run in CI & `tests/as_any_mut_verification.rs`).
  - Auto-fix helper: `scripts/add_as_any_mut.py` (use with caution and manual review).
- Feature flags are used heavily in `Cargo.toml` (e.g., `openblas`, `with_tch`, `python_bindings`, `safe_tensors`). Use `--features` when running builds/tests locally to match CI.
- Python ABI note: To build without a local Python interpreter, use `py_abi3` feature and set `PYO3_NO_PYTHON=1` (see `Cargo.toml` comments).

## How to add or change functionality (practical examples) 📚

- Adding an op (Rust):
  - Define the struct & implement `Operation` in `src/ops.rs`.
  - Add a wrapper method on `Tensor` in `src/tensor.rs` (e.g., `fn leaky_relu(&self, alpha: f32) -> Tensor`).
  - Add tests under `src/` (unit tests) and, if exposed to Python, a Python smoke test under `tests/` or an example in `examples/`.
- Adding a layer (Rust `Module`):
  - Add struct in `src/nn/*.rs`, implement `Module` trait and include weights in `parameters()`.
  - Ensure `as_any_mut` exists for the impl.

## Python integration notes (common gotchas) 🐍

- Slicing semantics and indexing implemented in `src/lib.rs` (`__getitem__`, `__setitem__`)—mirror numpy-like behavior; follow the existing approach when changing index handling.
- Use `maturin develop` to get an up-to-date dev wheel for running python smoke tests like `tests/python_smoke_test.py` or `tests/python_llava_smoke.py`.
- SafeTensors loader & helpers are in `src/io/safetensors_loader.rs` and examples like `examples/load_model.py` and `examples/convert_torch_to_safetensors.py` demonstrate common usage.

## Integration & external dependencies 🔗

- Optional crates and native libraries: OpenBLAS (for `openblas` feature), libtorch (for `with_tch`), tokenizers (feature `with_tokenizers`), and safetensors (feature `safe_tensors`).
- CI shows commands & setup for both Linux and Windows — follow it closely for platform-specific setup.

## Tests, benchmarks, and regression checks ✅

- Rust unit tests: `cargo test` (use features to exercise code paths).
- Python smoke tests: run `maturin develop` then `python tests/python_smoke_test.py` and `python tests/python_llava_smoke.py`.
- Benchmarks: `cargo bench` and CI uses scheduled workflows to update baseline reports (`.github/workflows/update-bench-baseline.yml`).

## Transformer notes & recent fixes 🔧

- Canonical implementation: **use `src/nn/transformer_cleaned.rs`** — it includes RoPE, NL-OOB, kv-head expansion, LLaMA-style pre-norm options, and robust `load_state_dict` handling.
- Compatibility: `src/io/safetensors_loader.rs::augment_state_dict_for_compat` maps many HF naming variants (e.g., `self_attn.q_proj.weight`, `mlp.gate_proj`) into internal names so `load_state_dict` can apply.
- Recent fix: the `Module` impl for `MultiHeadAttention` previously delegated to the trait methods (causing recursion). It now delegates to `parameters_impl`, `named_parameters_impl`, and `load_state_dict_impl` to avoid stack overflows.
- Guard test: `src/nn/tests/mha_impl_tests.rs` was added to check `parameters()`/`named_parameters()` delegation.

## Quick PR checklist ✅

- Run `python scripts/verify_as_any_mut.py` (or CI equivalent) to ensure `as_any_mut` is present in all `Module` impls.
- Run transformer tests: `cargo test src/nn/tests::transformer*`.
- Build Python wheel & smoke test (Linux/CI): `maturin develop --release && python tests/python_llava_smoke.py`.
- If changing state dict loading or key naming, add unit tests in `src/io/safetensors_loader.rs` and `src/nn/tests/`.

## Where to look when something breaks 🔍

- Build failures (Rust): `target/` logs and `cargo test --verbose` output; feature matrix mismatches are frequent causes.
- Python build errors: check maturin logs and ensure Python dev headers or `PYO3_NO_PYTHON` usage are correct.
- Shape/grad bugs: start in `src/tensor.rs` and `src/ops.rs`; tests in `src/nn/tests/` (e.g., transformer tests) cover many edge cases.

---

If anything above is unclear or you want more examples (e.g., a quick checklist for adding an op + exposing it to Python), tell me which area and I’ll iterate. Thanks! 🎯

Use includePattern to search within files matching a specific pattern, or in a specific file, using a relative path. Use 'includeIgnoredFiles' to include files normally ignored by .gitignore, other ignore files, and `files.exclude` and `search.exclude` settings. Warning: using this may cause the search to be slower, only set it when you want to search in ignored folders like node_modules or build outputs. Use this tool when you want to see an overview of a particular file, instead of using read_file many times to look for code within a file.

query.description: The pattern to search for in files in the workspace. Use regex with alternation (e.g., 'word1|word2|word3') or character classes to find multiple potential words in a single search. Be sure to set the isRegexp property properly to declare whether it's a regex or plain text pattern. Is case-insensitive.

isRegexp.description: Whether the pattern is a regex.

includePattern.description: Search files matching this glob pattern. Will be applied to the relative path of files within the workspace. To search recursively inside a folder, use a proper glob pattern like "src/folder/**". Do not use | in includePattern.

maxResults.description: The maximum number of results to return. Do not use this unless necessary, it can slow things down. By default, only some matches are returned. If you use this and don't see what you're looking for, you can try again with a more specific query or a larger maxResults.

includeIgnoredFiles.description: Whether to include files that would normally be ignored according to .gitignore, other ignore files and `files.exclude` and `search.exclude` settings. Warning: using this may cause the search to be slower. Only set it when you want to search in ignored folders like node_modules or build outputs.

Also use this tool after editing a file to validate the change.

tools.name: get_vscode_api
tools.description:
Get comprehensive VS Code API documentation and references for extension development. This tool provides authoritative documentation for VS Code's extensive API surface, including proposed APIs, contribution points, and best practices. Use this tool for understanding complex VS Code API interactions.

When to use this tool:
- User asks about specific VS Code APIs, interfaces, or extension capabilities
- Need documentation for VS Code extension contribution points (commands, views, settings, etc.)
- Questions about proposed APIs and their usage patterns
- Understanding VS Code extension lifecycle, activation events, and packaging
- Best practices for VS Code extension development architecture
- API examples and code patterns for extension features
- Troubleshooting extension-specific issues or API limitations

When NOT to use this tool:
- Creating simple standalone files or scripts unrelated to VS Code extensions
- General programming questions not specific to VS Code extension development
- Questions about using VS Code as an editor (user-facing features)
- Non-extension related development tasks
- File creation or editing that doesn't involve VS Code extension APIs

CRITICAL usage guidelines:
1. Always include specific API names, interfaces, or concepts in your query
2. Mention the extension feature you're trying to implement
3. Include context about proposed vs stable APIs when relevant
4. Reference specific contribution points when asking about extension manifest
5. Be specific about the VS Code version or API version when known

Scope: This tool is for EXTENSION DEVELOPMENT ONLY - building tools that extend VS Code itself, not for general file creation or non-extension programming tasks.

query.description: The query to search vscode documentation for. Should contain all relevant context.

tools.name: install_extension
tools.description: Install an extension in VS Code. Use this tool to install an extension in Visual Studio Code as part of a new workspace creation process only.

tools.name: list_code_usages
tools.description:
Request to list all usages (references, definitions, implementations etc) of a function, class, method, variable etc. Use this tool when 
1. Looking for a sample implementation of an interface or class
2. Checking how a function is used throughout the codebase.
3. Including and updating all usages when changing a function, method, or constructor

symbolName.description: The name of the symbol, such as a function name, class name, method name, variable name, etc.

filePaths.description: One or more file paths which likely contain the definition of the symbol. For instance the file which declares a class or function. This is optional but will speed up the invocation of this tool and improve the quality of its output.

tools.name: memory
tools.description: Store a fact about the codebase in memory, so that it can be used in future code generation or review tasks. The fact should be a clear and concise statement about the codebase conventions, structure, logic, or usage. It may be based on the code itself, or on information provided by the user.

subject.description: The topic to which this memory relates. 1-2 words. Examples: naming conventions, testing practices, documentation, logging, authentication, sanitization, error handling.

fact.description: A clear and short description of a fact about the codebase or a convention used in the codebase. Must be less than 200 characters. Examples: Use JWT for authentication. Follow PEP 257 docstring conventions. Use single quotes for strings in Python. Use Winston for logging.

citations.description: The source of this fact, such as a file and line number in the codebase (e.g., path/file.go:123). If the convention is not explicitly stated in the codebase, you can point at several examples that illustrate it, selecting the most diverse set of examples you can find (e.g. from multiple files or contexts). If the fact is based on user input, the citations should be User input: followed by the contents of the input.

reason.description: A clear and detailed explanation of the reason behind storing this fact. Must be at least 2-3 sentences long, and include which future tasks this fact will be useful for and why it is important to remember this fact.

category.description: The type of memory being stored. This can be bootstrap_and_build (info about how to bootstrap and build the project), user_preferences (preferences of the user, such as coding style, tabs vs. spaces, favorite libraries, etc.), general (file independent facts), or file_specific (information about a specific file in the codebase).

tools.name: multi_replace_string_in_file
tools.description: This tool allows you to apply multiple replace_string_in_file operations in a single call, which is more efficient than calling replace_string_in_file multiple times. It takes an array of replacement operations and applies them sequentially. Each replacement operation has the same parameters as replace_string_in_file: filePath, oldString, newString, and explanation. This tool is ideal when you need to make multiple edits across different files or multiple edits in the same file. The tool will provide a summary of successful and failed operations.

explanation.description: A brief explanation of what the multi-replace operation will accomplish.

replacements.description: An array of replacement operations to apply sequentially.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the file to edit.

oldString.description: The exact literal text to replace, preferably unescaped. Include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. If this string is not the exact literal text or does not match exactly, this replacement will fail.

newString.description: The exact literal text to replace `oldString` with, preferably unescaped. Provide the EXACT text. Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.

tools.name: open_simple_browser
tools.description: Preview a website or open a URL in the editor's Simple Browser. Useful for quickly viewing locally hosted websites, demos, or resources without leaving the coding environment.

Read the contents of a file.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the notebook file with the cell to run, or the URI of a untitled, not yet named, file, such as `untitled:Untitled-1.ipynb

tools.name: replace_string_in_file
tools.description:
This is a tool for making edits in an existing file in the workspace. For moving or renaming files, use run in terminal tool with the 'mv' command instead. For larger edits, split them into smaller edits and call the edit tool multiple times to ensure accuracy. Before editing, always ensure you have the context to understand the file's contents and context. To edit a file, provide: 1) filePath (absolute path), 2) oldString (MUST be the exact literal text to replace including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc), and 3) newString (MUST be the exact literal text to replace \`oldString\` with (also including all whitespace, indentation, newlines, and surrounding code etc.). Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.). Each use of this tool replaces exactly ONE occurrence of oldString.

CRITICAL for \`oldString\`: Must uniquely identify the single instance to change. Include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. If this string matches multiple locations, or does not match exactly, the tool will fail. Never use 'Lines 123-456 omitted' from summarized documents or ...existing code... comments in the oldString or newString.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the file to edit.

oldString.description: The exact literal text to replace, preferably unescaped. For single replacements (default), include at least 3 lines of context BEFORE and AFTER the target text, matching whitespace and indentation precisely. For multiple replacements, specify expected_replacements parameter. If this string is not the exact literal text (i.e. you escaped it) or does not match exactly, the tool will fail.

newString.description: The exact literal text to replace `old_string` with, preferably unescaped. Provide the EXACT text. Ensure the resulting code is correct and idiomatic.

tools.name: run_notebook_cell

Code cells should be run as they are added or edited when working through a problem to bring the kernel state up to date and ensure the code executes successfully. Code cells are ready to run and don't require any pre-processing. If asked to run the first cell in a notebook, you should run the first code cell since markdown cells cannot be executed. NOTE: Avoid executing Markdown cells or providing Markdown cell IDs, as Markdown cells cannot be  executed.

filePath.description: An absolute path to the notebook file with the cell to run, or the URI of a untitled, not yet named, file, such as `untitled:Untitled-1.ipynb

tools.name: switch_agent
tools.description:
Switch to the Plan agent before exploring the codebase and refining implementation of a feature. The Plan agent provides specialized tools to explore the codebase, understand system architecture, and iterate with the user through clarifying questions and context gathering.

PLAN AGENT BEHAVIOR:
The Plan agent is a specialized assistant designed for research, exploration, and planning. It:
- Has access to powerful codebase exploration tools (search, read files, list directories, find symbols)
- Can ask clarifying questions to understand requirements better
- Proposes implementation approaches and validates them with the user
- Gathers comprehensive context before suggesting changes
- Handles complex, multi-file refactoring and architectural decisions
- Summarizes findings and creates detailed plans for implementation

EXAMPLES OF WHEN TO SWITCH TO PLAN:
- "I want to refactor the data flow in this component" → Plan can explore the component dependencies
- "How should I integrate this new feature?" → Plan can investigate the architecture and propose approaches
- "Find all usages of this pattern and suggest a better way" → Plan can search comprehensively and report findings
- "I need to migrate from X to Y" → Plan can understand current structure and propose migration strategy

USE THIS TOOL IMMEDIATELY AND PROACTIVELY BEFORE ANY OTHER TOOL CALLS OR CODE EXPLORATION WHEN:
- The user's request is ambiguous, underspecified, or could be interpreted multiple ways
- You need to explore the codebase, gather context, or understand the architecture - CODE EXPLORATION IS THE PLAN AGENT'S PRIMARY RESPONSIBILITY
- The task involves multiple files, complex refactoring, or architectural decisions
- You want to propose an approach and validate it with the user before implementing
- The user explicitly asks for a plan or wants to discuss the approach first
- You're uncertain whether you have sufficient context to confidently implement the complete change

CRITICAL: If you are about to call any code exploration tools (readFile, findTextInFiles, searchCodebase, listDirectory, etc.), STOP immediately and switch to the Plan agent first. Code exploration, context gathering, and architectural understanding belong to the Plan agent, not the inline editor.

You should ONLY skip using this tool when:
- The task is completely straightforward with explicit, detailed implementation instructions
- You already have complete and specific context about exactly what needs to change and where
- The user has explicitly instructed you to skip planning and just make the change

agentName.description: The name of the agent to switch to. Currently only 'Plan' is supported.

The model should use this tool whenever it needs to discover extensions or resolve information about known ones. To use the tool, the model has to provide the category of the extensions, relevant search keywords, or known extension IDs. Note that search results may include false positives, so reviewing and filtering is recommended.

isBackground.description: Whether the task runs in the background without blocking the UI or other tasks. Set to true for long-running processes like watch tasks or servers that should continue executing without requiring user attention. When false, the task will block the terminal until completion.

Can be a predefined matcher like '$tsc' (TypeScript), '$eslint - stylish', '$gcc', etc., or a custom pattern defined in tasks.json. This helps VS Code display errors in the Problems panel and enables quick navigation to error locations.

tools.name: manage_todo_list
tools.description:
Manage a structured todo list to track progress and plan tasks throughout your coding session. Use this tool VERY frequently to ensure task visibility and proper planning.

When to use this tool:
- Complex multi-step work requiring planning and tracking
- When user provides multiple tasks or requests (numbered/comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions that require multiple steps
- BEFORE starting work on any todo (mark as in-progress)
- IMMEDIATELY after completing each todo (mark completed individually)
- When breaking down larger tasks into smaller actionable steps
- To give users visibility into your progress and planning

When NOT to use:
- Single, trivial tasks that can be completed in one step
- Purely conversational/informational requests
- When just reading files or performing simple searches

CRITICAL workflow:
1. Plan tasks by writing todo list with specific, actionable items
2. Mark ONE todo as in-progress before starting work
3. Complete the work for that specific todo
4. Mark that todo as completed IMMEDIATELY
5. Move to next todo and repeat

Todo states:
- not-started: Todo not yet begun
- in-progress: Currently working (limit ONE at a time)
- completed: Finished successfully

IMPORTANT: Mark todos completed as soon as they are done. Do not batch completions.

todoList.description: Complete array of all todo items. Must include ALL items - both existing and new.

id.description: Unique identifier for the todo. Use sequential numbers starting from 1.

title.description: Concise action-oriented todo label (3-7 words). Displayed in UI.

status.description: not-started: Not begun | in-progress: Currently working (max 1) | completed: Fully finished with no blockers

tools.name: run_in_terminal
tools.description:
This tool allows you to execute PowerShell commands in a persistent terminal session, preserving environment variables, working directory, and other context across multiple commands.

Command Execution:
- Prefer ; when chaining commands on one line
- Prefer pipelines | for object-based data flow
- Never create a sub-shell (eg. powershell -c "command") unless explicitly asked

Directory Management:
- Prefer relative paths when navigating directories, only use absolute when the path is far away or the current cwd is not expected
- Remember when isBackground=false is specified, that the shell and cwd are reused until it is moved to the background
- Use $PWD or Get-Location for current directory
- Use Push-Location/Pop-Location for directory stack

Program Execution:
- Supports .NET, Python, Node.js, and other executables
- Install modules via Install-Module, Install-Package
- Use Get-Command to verify cmdlet/function availability

Background Processes:
- For long-running tasks (e.g., servers), set isBackground=true
- Returns a terminal ID for checking status and runtime later
- Use Start-Job for background PowerShell jobs

Output Management:
- Output is automatically truncated if longer than 60KB to prevent context overflow
- Use Select-Object, Where-Object, Format-Table to filter output
- Use -First/-Last parameters to limit results
- For pager commands, add | Out-String or | Format-List

Best Practices:
- Use proper cmdlet names instead of aliases in scripts
- Quote paths with spaces: "C:\Path With Spaces"
- Prefer PowerShell cmdlets over external commands when available
- Prefer idiomatic PowerShell like Get-ChildItem instead of dir or ls for file listings
- Use Test-Path to check file/directory existence
- Be specific with Select-Object properties to avoid excessive output
- Avoid printing credentials unless absolutely required

command.description: The command to run in the terminal.

explanation.description: A one-sentence description of what the command does. This will be shown to the user before the command is run.

goal.description: A short description of the goal or purpose of the command (e.g., "Install dependencies", "Start development server").

isBackground.description:
Whether the command starts a background process.

- If true, a new shell will be spawned where the cwd is the workspace directory and will run asynchronously in the background and you will not see the output.

- If false, a single shell is shared between all non-background terminals where the cwd starts at the workspace directory and is remembered until that terminal is moved to the background, the tool call will block on the command finishing and only then you will get the output.

Examples of background processes: building in watch mode, starting a server. You can check the output of a background process later on by using get_terminal_output.

timeout.description: An optional timeout in milliseconds. When provided, the tool will stop tracking the command after this duration and return the output collected so far. Be conservative with the timeout duration, give enough time that the command would complete on a low-end machine. Use 0 for no timeout. If it's not clear how long the command will take then use 0 to avoid prematurely terminating it, never guess too low.

tools.name: runSubagent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks autonomously. This tool is good at researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries, use this agent to perform the search for you.

- Agents do not run async or in the background, you will wait for the agent's result.
- When the agent is done, it will return a single message back to you. The result returned by the agent is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Each agent invocation is stateless. You will not be able to send additional messages to the agent, nor will the agent be able to communicate with you outside of its final report. Therefore, your prompt should contain a highly detailed task description for the agent to perform autonomously and you should specify exactly what information the agent should return back to you in its final and only message to you.
- The agent's outputs should generally be trusted
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since it is not aware of the user's intent
- If the user asks for a certain agent, you MUST provide that EXACT agent name (case-sensitive) to invoke that specific agent.

prompt.description: A detailed description of the task for the agent to perform

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

agentName.description: Optional name of a specific agent to invoke. If not provided, uses the current agent.

tools.name: terminal_last_command
tools.description: Get the last command run in the active terminal.

tools.name: terminal_selection
tools.description: Get the current selection in the active terminal.

tools.name: activate_data_analysis_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is designed to facilitate efficient data analysis workflows. The primary focus is on ensuring that users follow best practices when analyzing data files, starting with the 'data_analysis_best_practice' tool. This tool provides a foundational understanding of the analysis workflow, which is crucial before utilizing any other tools in this group. The 'check_panel_open' tool allows users to verify if a 'Data Viewer' panel is currently active, providing essential information about the data source and its status. 

Once the panel status is confirmed, users can leverage the 'get_table_schema' tool to retrieve the structure of the data, including metadata such as row and column counts, names, and inferred data types. This is particularly useful for understanding the dataset before performing any operations. The 'read_rows' tool enables users to extract specific rows from the data, either from the open panel or directly from a file, with options for filtering columns, making it easy to focus on relevant information. 

For users looking to save their analysis results, the 'export_panel_data' tool allows for exporting the current data state to a designated folder in the workspace, ensuring that data can be preserved for future reference or further analysis. This tool also respects the original file format, maintaining consistency in data handling. 

Together, these tools create a cohesive suite for data analysis, guiding users through the necessary steps to ensure thorough and accurate data examination, while also providing mechanisms for data management and export.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: activate_ai_agent_evaluation_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is focused on the evaluation and development of AI agents and applications. It provides a structured approach to converting declarative agent specifications into executable code, ensuring that best practices are followed during the coding process. The 'convert_declarative_agent_to_code' tool is essential for developers looking to translate their specifications into runnable code, offering guidance and code samples in Python or .NET. 

The 'evaluation_planner' tool serves as a critical starting point for any evaluation process, guiding users through a multi-turn conversation to clarify essential details such as evaluation metrics, test datasets, and runtime requirements. This ensures that all necessary information is gathered before proceeding with evaluation code generation. 

Once the planning phase is complete, users can utilize the 'get_evaluation_code_gen_best_practices' tool to access best practices specifically tailored for generating evaluation code, ensuring that the evaluation process is both effective and efficient. Additionally, the 'get_agent_model_code_sample' tool provides valuable code snippets for AI agent and model development, facilitating quicker implementation and reducing the likelihood of errors. 

Lastly, the 'get_tracing_code_gen_best_practices' tool offers guidance on best practices for tracing operations within AI applications, which is crucial for debugging and performance monitoring. Collectively, these tools empower developers to create, evaluate, and refine AI agents with a focus on best practices and structured methodologies.

Be sure to call this tool if you need a capability related to the above.

tools.name: ai-mlstudio-get_trend_data
tools.description: Gets the evaluation trend data from the currently focused Evaluation Trend Analysis view (either standalone panel or embedded trend in Data Viewer). Returns: dataPoints (array of files with fileName, filePath, and metrics - metric values are AVERAGED across selected rows), selectedMetrics (list of metrics being compared), jsonArrayProperty (for JSON files, indicates which array property the data comes from), selectedRows (1-based row indices used for averaging, undefined means all rows), totalRows (total row count). Use this tool when the user asks to analyze or discuss evaluation trends. The tool automatically detects which trend view is currently active/focused.

tools.name: activate_migration_assessment_tools
tools.description:
Call this tool when you need access to a new category of tools. The category of tools is described as follows:

This group of tools is designed to facilitate the assessment and reporting of migration readiness and outcomes. The 'migration_assessmentReport' tool provides a detailed webview interface that displays the results of a migration assessment, including identified issues, recommendations for improvement, and an analysis of readiness for Azure migration. This tool is essential for users to understand the implications of their migration efforts and to plan accordingly based on the assessment results.

The 'migration_assessmentReportsList' tool complements the first by allowing users to access a list of all assessment reports generated. This is particularly useful for tracking multiple assessments over time, enabling users to compare results and monitor progress in addressing identified issues.

Lastly, the 'uploadAssessSummaryReport' tool serves as a means to upload the summary report of the assessment to a GitHub issue. This integration allows for seamless collaboration and documentation of the migration process, ensuring that all stakeholders have access to the assessment findings and can contribute to discussions or resolutions.

Together, these tools create a comprehensive workflow for managing migration assessments, from initial evaluation to reporting and collaboration. tools.name: mcp_copilot_upgra_upgrade_authenticate_nuget_feed
tools.description:
Call upgrade_authenticate_nuget_feed to resolve NuGet package authentication failures when restore or build operations fail with access errors.

**When to use this tool:**
- Build or restore operations fail with authentication errors for private NuGet feeds
- Error messages contain NU1301 (unable to load service index for source)
- HTTP 401 (Unauthorized) or 403 (Forbidden) errors when accessing NuGet feeds
- Errors mention "Unable to find package" from Azure DevOps feeds (pkgs.dev.azure.com)
- Package restore fails with "Unable to load the service index" from authenticated feeds

**How this tool works (requires human-in-the-loop):**
1. Invokes the Azure Artifacts credential provider in interactive mode
2. The credential provider outputs authentication instructions (typically a device code and URL)
3. User must manually open the provided URL in a browser and complete authentication
4. After user completes authentication, call this tool again to verify credentials are cached
5. Once credentials are verified, retry the failed operation

**Important:** This tool does NOT automatically open a browser. It provides instructions that the user must follow manually. After the user authenticates, you must call this tool again to verify the credentials are properly cached before retrying the build.

Extract the failing feed URL from error messages to use as the feedUrl parameter.

# Copilot instructions for Tensor-Engine

## Quick orientation ✅

- Languages: **Rust** core (crate: `tensor_engine`) + **Python** bindings (PyO3/maturin). See `Cargo.toml`, `src/`, and `src/lib.rs`.
- High-level architecture: core tensor/autograd in `src/tensor.rs`, ops in `src/ops.rs`, NN layers in `src/nn/*.rs`, IO & loaders in `src/io/*` (SafeTensors and PyTorch loaders), Python surface in `src/lib.rs`.
- Primary patterns to follow: `Module` and `Operation` traits, and PyO3 style wrappers (`PyTensor` in `src/lib.rs`).

## Immediate developer workflows (commands you’ll use) 🔧

- Run unit tests (Rust):
  - cargo test --verbose --workspace
  - For feature matrix: cargo test --verbose --workspace --features "<feature>"
- Build & iterate Python bindings locally (recommended):
  - pip install maturin
  - maturin develop --release --bindings pyo3
  - Build wheel: maturin build --release
- CI-specific notes (see `.github/workflows/ci.yml`):
  - OpenBLAS support via feature `openblas` (Windows CI sets OPENBLAS_DIR)
  - `with_tch` feature needs a compatible libtorch / VC toolchain on Windows
- Docs: build with MkDocs (`scripts/build_docs.ps1` or `./scripts/build_docs.sh`) and preview with `mkdocs serve`.

## Project-specific conventions & rules (must follow) ⚠️

- impl Module must provide `fn as_any_mut(&mut self) -> &mut dyn Any`.
  - Verification: `python scripts/verify_as_any_mut.py` (also run in CI & `tests/as_any_mut_verification.rs`).
  - Auto-fix helper: `scripts/add_as_any_mut.py` (use with caution and manual review).
- Feature flags are used heavily in `Cargo.toml` (e.g., `openblas`, `with_tch`, `python_bindings`, `safe_tensors`). Use `--features` when running builds/tests locally to match CI.
- Python ABI note: To build without a local Python interpreter, use `py_abi3` feature and set `PYO3_NO_PYTHON=1` (see `Cargo.toml` comments).

## How to add or change functionality (practical examples) 📚

- Adding an op (Rust):
  - Define the struct & implement `Operation` in `src/ops.rs`.
  - Add a wrapper method on `Tensor` in `src/tensor.rs` (e.g., `fn leaky_relu(&self, alpha: f32) -> Tensor`).
  - Add tests under `src/` (unit tests) and, if exposed to Python, a Python smoke test under `tests/` or an example in `examples/`.
- Adding a layer (Rust `Module`):
  - Add struct in `src/nn/*.rs`, implement `Module` trait and include weights in `parameters()`.
  - Ensure `as_any_mut` exists for the impl.

## Python integration notes (common gotchas) 🐍

- Slicing semantics and indexing implemented in `src/lib.rs` (`__getitem__`, `__setitem__`)—mirror numpy-like behavior; follow the existing approach when changing index handling.
- Use `maturin develop` to get an up-to-date dev wheel for running python smoke tests like `tests/python_smoke_test.py` or `tests/python_llava_smoke.py`.
- SafeTensors loader & helpers are in `src/io/safetensors_loader.rs` and examples like `examples/load_model.py` and `examples/convert_torch_to_safetensors.py` demonstrate common usage.

## Integration & external dependencies 🔗

- Optional crates and native libraries: OpenBLAS (for `openblas` feature), libtorch (for `with_tch`), tokenizers (feature `with_tokenizers`), and safetensors (feature `safe_tensors`).
- CI shows commands & setup for both Linux and Windows — follow it closely for platform-specific setup.

## Tests, benchmarks, and regression checks ✅

- Rust unit tests: `cargo test` (use features to exercise code paths).
- Python smoke tests: run `maturin develop` then `python tests/python_smoke_test.py` and `python tests/python_llava_smoke.py`.
- Benchmarks: `cargo bench` and CI uses scheduled workflows to update baseline reports (`.github/workflows/update-bench-baseline.yml`).

## Transformer notes & recent fixes 🔧

- Canonical implementation: **use `src/nn/transformer_cleaned.rs`** — it includes RoPE, NL-OOB, kv-head expansion, LLaMA-style pre-norm options, and robust `load_state_dict` handling.
- Compatibility: `src/io/safetensors_loader.rs::augment_state_dict_for_compat` maps many HF naming variants (e.g., `self_attn.q_proj.weight`, `mlp.gate_proj`) into internal names so `load_state_dict` can apply.
- Recent fix: the `Module` impl for `MultiHeadAttention` previously delegated to the trait methods (causing recursion). It now delegates to `parameters_impl`, `named_parameters_impl`, and `load_state_dict_impl` to avoid stack overflows.
- Guard test: `src/nn/tests/mha_impl_tests.rs` was added to check `parameters()`/`named_parameters()` delegation.

## Quick PR checklist ✅

- Run `python scripts/verify_as_any_mut.py` (or CI equivalent) to ensure `as_any_mut` is present in all `Module` impls.
- Run transformer tests: `cargo test src/nn/tests::transformer*`.
- Build Python wheel & smoke test (Linux/CI): `maturin develop --release && python tests/python_llava_smoke.py`.
- If changing state dict loading or key naming, add unit tests in `src/io/safetensors_loader.rs` and `src/nn/tests/`.

## Where to look when something breaks 🔍

- Build failures (Rust): `target/` logs and `cargo test --verbose` output; feature matrix mismatches are frequent causes.
- Python build errors: check maturin logs and ensure Python dev headers or `PYO3_NO_PYTHON` usage are correct.
- Shape/grad bugs: start in `src/tensor.rs` and `src/ops.rs`; tests in `src/nn/tests/` (e.g., transformer tests) cover many edge cases.

---

If anything above is unclear or you want more examples (e.g., a quick checklist for adding an op + exposing it to Python), tell me which area and I’ll iterate. Thanks! 🎯
